questions.stem: A patient is being discharged on prednisone 40 mg daily for 10 days following an acute COPD exacerbation. Which statement by the patient indicates that ADDITIONAL teaching is needed?

options.text: 'I should not stop this medication suddenly without talking to my doctor.'
'I can stop taking this medication early if I start feeling better.'
'I should monitor my blood sugar more closely while taking this medication.'
'I should take this medication in the morning with food.'

questions.rationale: Stopping corticosteroids abruptly or early is dangerous and incorrect. Even a 10-day course suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and requires a tapering strategy if used longer, and should always be completed as prescribed for a short course. Early discontinuation risks adrenal insufficiency and relapse of the condition being treated. The patient should understand that the full course must be completed, and that stopping suddenly (in longer courses) can cause an adrenal crisis. Statement A is correct — do not stop without medical advice. Statement C is correct — steroids cause hyperglycemia. Statement D is correct — morning administration mimics cortisol's natural diurnal rhythm and reduces GI upset.
questions.takeaway: Corticosteroid teaching: complete the full course, do not stop early or abruptly. Monitor blood glucose. Take in morning with food. Know signs of infection (immunosuppression). Report mood changes, edema, GI symptoms.
questions.editorial_notes: source-rotation: selected from the NCLEX review-batch library with recent-family avoidance.

questions.stem: A nurse is completing an admission assessment on a 79-year-old patient transferred from a nursing facility. Which combination of factors identifies the HIGHEST fall risk?

options.text: Age >65 and female gender
History of fall in the past 6 months, taking 3 antihypertensive medications, and orthostatic hypotension (systolic drop >20 mmHg on standing)
Mild bilateral hearing loss and BMI of 29
Mild arthritis in both knees and occasional evening confusion

questions.rationale: The highest fall risk constellation combines: (1) Prior fall history — the single strongest predictor of future falls in the elderly; (2) Polypharmacy with antihypertensives — alpha-blockers, diuretics, and calcium channel blockers commonly cause orthostatic hypotension and syncope; (3) Documented orthostatic hypotension — directly causes dizziness and falls upon position change. Both the Morse Fall Scale and STRATIFY risk tool weight prior falls most heavily. Key interventions: bed in lowest position, non-skid footwear, call light within reach, scheduled toileting (most falls occur during nighttime toileting), orthostatic vital signs before ambulation, and urgent medication review. Age and gender alone are poor predictors without functional factors.
questions.takeaway: Highest fall risk: prior fall + polypharmacy (antihypertensives) + orthostatic hypotension. Prior fall is the strongest single predictor. Target modifiable risk factors aggressively.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old patient with hypertension, chronic insomnia, chronic pain, depression, and GERD takes: amlodipine, diphenhydramine (for sleep), amitriptyline, ibuprofen, and omeprazole. Using Beers Criteria principles, which medications present the GREATEST risk for this elderly patient?

options.text: Omeprazole and amlodipine — both increase fall risk and should be avoided in elderly
Diphenhydramine and amitriptyline — both are highly anticholinergic and explicitly listed as inappropriate in the AGS Beers Criteria
Ibuprofen alone — GI bleeding is the only significant concern in this patient
Amlodipine and ibuprofen — calcium channel blockers are contraindicated over age 80

questions.rationale: The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria identifies medications potentially inappropriate in adults ≥65. Diphenhydramine (first-generation antihistamine) and amitriptyline (tricyclic antidepressant) are both strongly anticholinergic and explicitly listed as 'avoid' in elderly. Anticholinergic effects (cumulative burden): cognitive impairment, delirium, urinary retention, constipation, dry mouth, tachycardia, blurred vision, and increased fall risk. Amitriptyline additionally causes orthostatic hypotension (fall risk), cardiac conduction abnormalities, and QT prolongation. Additional concerns in this patient: ibuprofen (NSAID) — risk of GI bleeding (especially with GERD), renal impairment, and cardiovascular events (also Beers listed — prefer acetaminophen). Safer alternatives: melatonin or low-dose doxepin for insomnia; SSRIs/SNRIs for depression (avoid TCAs); acetaminophen for pain.

distractorRationales.a: The option can leave bleeding or anticoagulation injury untreated because it answers a lower-acuity part of the scenario. "Diphenhydramine and amitriptyline — both are highly anticholinergic and explicitly listed as inappropriate in the AGS" fits the safer response to the cue "An 83-year-old patient with hypertension, chronic insomnia, chronic pain, depression".
distractorRationales.c: The option can leave bleeding or anticoagulation injury untreated because it answers a lower-acuity part of the scenario. "Diphenhydramine and amitriptyline — both are highly anticholinergic and explicitly listed as inappropriate in the AGS" fits the safer response to the cue "Additional concerns in this patient: ibuprofen (NSAID) — risk of GI bleeding (especially with GERD), renal impairment".
distractorRationales.d: The safer response addresses bleeding or anticoagulation injury; "Amlodipine and ibuprofen — calcium channel blockers are contraindicated over age 80" moves care toward routine care before bleeding-risk intervention.

questions.takeaway: Beers Criteria: anticholinergics (diphenhydramine, TCAs like amitriptyline) are highest risk in elderly — cause delirium, falls, urinary retention. NSAIDs also Beers-listed. Review medications at every hospitalization.

questions.stem: A public health nurse identifies a patient who recently converted to a positive PPD (tuberculin skin test) after a negative test 6 months ago. Chest X-ray is negative. The patient has no symptoms. What is the recommended follow-up management?

options.text: Repeat the PPD in 3 months to confirm conversion
No treatment needed — latent TB does not require intervention if the patient is asymptomatic
Initiate INH (isoniazid) prophylaxis for 9 months; monitor monthly for hepatotoxicity
Start a 4-drug RIPE regimen (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for active TB

questions.rationale: A recent PPD conversion (negative → positive within 2 years) with negative chest X-ray indicates latent TB infection (LTBI). Treatment of LTBI prevents progression to active TB (10% lifetime risk, higher in immunocompromised patients). First-line LTBI regimens: (1) INH daily × 9 months (9H) — standard; (2) Rifapentine + INH weekly × 12 weeks (3HP) — shorter, increasingly preferred; (3) Rifampin daily × 4 months. INH monitoring: monthly clinical evaluation for hepatotoxicity symptoms (jaundice, nausea, fatigue, RUQ pain); baseline LFTs for high-risk patients; hold INH if AST >3× ULN with symptoms or >5× ULN asymptomatic. 4-drug RIPE is for active TB, not LTBI.

distractorRationales.a: The option can leave medication toxicity untreated because it moves to activity, intake, or discharge planning too early. "Initiate INH (isoniazid) prophylaxis for 9 months; monitor monthly for hepatotoxicity" fits the safer response to the cue "Treatment of LTBI prevents progression to active TB (10% lifetime risk, higher in immunocompromised patients)".
distractorRationales.b: "No treatment needed — latent TB does not require intervention if the patient is asymptomatic" moves to activity, intake, or discharge planning too early. The cue "First-line LTBI regimens: (1) INH daily × 9 months (9H) — standard" raises concern for medication toxicity, so medication-safety intervention is needed before ambulation, intake, or discharge teaching.
distractorRationales.d: This distractor shifts care toward misprioritization instead of medication-safety intervention. The stem cue "A public health nurse identifies a patient who recently converted to a positive PPD (tuberculin skin test) after" makes medication toxicity the active safety concern.

questions.takeaway: Recent PPD conversion + negative CXR = LTBI → INH prophylaxis 9 months (or 3HP 12 weeks); monitor monthly for INH hepatotoxicity; 4-drug RIPE is for active TB only.

questions.stem: A patient with untreated hyperthyroidism is admitted postoperatively with HR 148 bpm (AF), temperature 39.8°C, BP 158/92 mmHg, and extreme agitation. The nurse suspects thyroid storm. Which medication sequence reflects the CORRECT pharmacological management priority?

options.text: Propylthiouracil (PTU) first → then potassium iodide → then propranolol → then glucocorticoid
Methimazole first → then radioactive iodine → then atenolol
Propranolol first → then PTU → then potassium iodide → then hydrocortisone
Potassium iodide first → then PTU → then propranolol

questions.rationale: Thyroid storm management follows a specific pharmacological sequence to block thyroid hormone synthesis and release: (1) PTU first — blocks new hormone synthesis AND peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion (this is why PTU is preferred over methimazole in storm). (2) Potassium iodide (Lugol's) given 1 hour AFTER PTU — blocks thyroid hormone release (the Wolff-Chaikoff effect). Giving iodine before the antithyroid drug would paradoxically worsen hormone synthesis. (3) Propranolol — controls adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, hypertension, tremor). (4) Glucocorticoids (hydrocortisone/dexamethasone) — reduce peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion and prevent relative adrenal insufficiency. Radioactive iodine is NOT used in thyroid storm — it is an elective outpatient treatment.

distractorRationales.b: The cue "(4) Glucocorticoids (hydrocortisone/dexamethasone) — reduce peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion and prevent relative adrenal insufficiency" suggests medication toxicity, so "Methimazole first → then radioactive iodine → then atenolol" would not correct the active problem. Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.
distractorRationales.c: "Propranolol first → then PTU → then potassium iodide → then hydrocortisone" misses the bedside risk. The cue "(4) Glucocorticoids (hydrocortisone/dexamethasone) — reduce peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion and prevent relative adrenal insufficiency" points to medication toxicity. Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.
distractorRationales.d: "Potassium iodide first → then PTU → then propranolol" misses the bedside risk. The cue "(3) Propranolol — controls adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, hypertension, tremor)" points to medication toxicity. Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.

questions.takeaway: Thyroid storm Rx sequence: PTU → (wait 1h) → Potassium iodide → Propranolol → Hydrocortisone. KEY: PTU BEFORE iodine (blocking synthesis before blocking release). Never give iodine first — it can fuel more hormone synthesis if the gland isn't blocked.

questions.stem: A patient presents with BP 218/130 mmHg, severe headache, blurred vision, and confusion. Fundoscopic exam shows papilledema. Urinalysis shows proteinuria and hematuria. Which condition is present and what is the correct blood pressure management approach?

options.text: Hypertensive urgency — oral labetalol and discharge home with follow-up
Hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension) — lower MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour using IV antihypertensives, with careful monitoring for ischemia
Hypertensive emergency — lower BP rapidly to < 120/80 mmHg within 1 hour to prevent further end-organ damage
Severe hypertension without emergency — reassess BP after 30 minutes of rest before intervening

questions.rationale: This patient has hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension) — severely elevated BP with end-organ damage: neurological (headache, confusion, papilledema = hypertensive encephalopathy), renal (proteinuria, hematuria). This requires IV antihypertensives (labetalol, nicardipine, or clevidipine) with arterial line monitoring. The critical teaching point: do NOT lower BP too rapidly. The target is to reduce MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour. Organs autoregulate to high-pressure environments — a rapid drop can cause ischemic stroke, MI, or renal infarction as perfusion pressure suddenly falls. Hypertensive urgency has severe elevation but NO end-organ damage — treated with oral agents over hours to days.

distractorRationales.a: This distractor shifts care toward premature activity instead of neurologic safety assessment. The stem cue "A patient presents with BP 218/130 mmHg, severe headache, blurred vision" makes neurologic deterioration the active safety concern.
distractorRationales.c: This distractor shifts care toward premature attribution instead of neurologic safety assessment. The stem cue "A patient presents with BP 218/130 mmHg, severe headache, blurred vision" makes neurologic deterioration the active safety concern.
distractorRationales.d: The safer response addresses neurologic deterioration; "Severe hypertension without emergency — reassess BP after 30 minutes of rest before intervening" moves care toward routine observation before neurologic safety assessment.

questions.takeaway: Hypertensive emergency: severe HTN + end-organ damage = IV antihypertensives, reduce MAP ≤ 25% in hour 1. Then 160/100 over 2-6h. Then normalize over 24-48h. Rapid BP lowering causes ischemia — the brain has autoregulated UP.

questions.stem: A patient who delivered 2 hours ago reports sudden, severe perineal pain and pressure. The nurse inspects the perineum and notes a 4 cm tense, purple, fluctuant mass on the right labia. What does this indicate, and what is the priority nursing action?

options.text: Normal postpartum edema; apply ice pack and reassure the patient
Vulvar hematoma; notify the provider immediately and monitor vital signs
Episiotomy dehiscence; apply sterile dressing and call the surgeon
Bartholin's cyst; apply warm compresses

questions.rationale: A tense, purple, fluctuant (fluid-filled), rapidly expanding perineal mass with severe pain is a vulvar hematoma — accumulation of blood in soft tissue from injured blood vessels, often after vaginal delivery or episiotomy. Small hematomas (<3–4 cm) may be managed conservatively with ice and observation; larger or expanding hematomas require surgical incision and evacuation. The immediate nursing priority is to notify the provider, monitor vital signs for hemodynamic compromise, and apply an ice pack for comfort. Normal edema (A) is soft, not fluctuant or purple. Episiotomy dehiscence (C) would show wound separation. A Bartholin's cyst (D) is not a postpartum complication.

distractorRationales.a: "Normal postpartum edema; apply ice pack and reassure the patient" misses the bedside risk. The cue "A patient who delivered 2 hours ago reports sudden, severe perineal pain and pressure" points to bleeding or anticoagulation injury. Bleeding risk requires assessment and source control before comfort measures, teaching, or routine medication timing.

The cue "A patient who delivered 2 hours ago reports sudden, severe perineal pain and pressure" raises concern for bleeding or anticoagulation injury, so bleeding-risk intervention is needed before waiting for a callback.
distractorRationales.d: The safer response addresses bleeding or anticoagulation injury; "Bartholin's cyst; apply warm compresses" moves care toward routine care before bleeding-risk intervention.

questions.stem: A home health nurse is assessing fall risk in a 78-year-old patient living independently. The patient completes the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test in 16 seconds. How should the nurse interpret this result and what intervention is indicated?

options.text: TUG <20 seconds is normal for age; no intervention needed
TUG ≥12 seconds indicates increased fall risk; refer to physical therapy and implement a fall prevention program
TUG is only valid in a clinical setting; results cannot be applied to home fall risk
TUG >30 seconds indicates fall risk; 16 seconds is normal

questions.rationale: The Timed Up and Go (TUG) test measures functional mobility: the patient rises from a standard chair, walks 3 meters, turns, walks back, and sits down. Scoring: <10 seconds = freely mobile, low fall risk; 10–19 seconds = mostly independent but increased fall risk; 20–29 seconds = variable mobility, moderate fall risk; ≥30 seconds = impaired mobility, high fall risk and need for assistance. A TUG of 16 seconds places this patient in the moderate fall risk category, warranting physical therapy referral, home safety assessment (remove throw rugs, install grab bars), medication review (sedatives, antihypertensives), and fall prevention education.

distractorRationales.a: This distractor shifts care toward false reassurance instead of medication-safety intervention. The stem cue "≥30 seconds = impaired mobility, high fall risk and need for assistance" makes medication toxicity the active safety concern.
distractorRationales.c: The cue "Scoring: <10 seconds = freely mobile, low fall risk" suggests medication toxicity, so "TUG is only valid in a clinical setting; results cannot be applied to home fall risk" would not correct the active problem. Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.
distractorRationales.d: The cue "Scoring: <10 seconds = freely mobile, low fall risk" suggests medication toxicity, so "TUG >30 seconds indicates fall risk; 16 seconds is normal" would not correct the active problem. Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.

questions.takeaway: TUG test: <10s = low risk; 10–19s = increased risk; ≥20s = moderate-high risk. TUG ≥12 seconds in elderly → fall risk; refer to PT, home safety assessment.

questions.stem: A nurse discovers that a colleague has been diverting controlled substances — taking opioids from the medication dispensing cabinet that are charted as wasted but are not being wasted appropriately. The colleague appears to be under the influence during a shift. Which action is the nurse's ethical and legal obligation?

options.text: Speak privately with the colleague and give them a chance to self-report before taking action
Document the suspicion in a personal diary for future reference if the behavior continues
Report immediately to the charge nurse and nursing supervisor, following facility policy for suspected substance diversion
Contact the State Board of Nursing directly to file a formal complaint without involving hospital administration

questions.rationale: Suspected drug diversion by a healthcare colleague must be reported immediately through the chain of command — charge nurse and supervisor — per facility policy. This protects patient safety (a potentially impaired nurse poses immediate risk), fulfills the nurse's ethical obligation under the ANA Code of Ethics, and triggers the appropriate investigation process. Giving the colleague time to self-report (A) delays patient safety action and may allow evidence destruction. Personal documentation (B) does not fulfill the reporting obligation. Going directly to the State BON (D) bypasses the facility process, which should occur first — BON involvement follows internal reporting.

distractorRationales.a: "Speak privately with the colleague and give them a chance to self-report before taking action" commits to a competing cause before checking the dangerous pattern. The cue "Giving the colleague time to self-report (A) delays patient safety action and may allow evidence destruction" raises concern for medication toxicity, so medication-safety intervention is needed before diagnostic reassurance.

distractorRationales.d: "Contact the State Board of Nursing directly to file a formal complaint without involving hospital administration" misses the bedside risk. The cue "This protects patient safety (a potentially impaired nurse poses immediate risk), fulfills the nurse's ethical obligation under the" points to medication toxicity. Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.

questions.stem: A nurse is with a patient who suddenly begins experiencing a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. What is the PRIORITY nursing action during the seizure?

options.text: Insert an oral airway to prevent tongue biting and aspiration
Restrain the patient's limbs to prevent injury
Protect the patient's head, clear the environment of hazards, turn the patient on their side, and time the seizure
Administer diazepam 10 mg IV immediately per standing orders

questions.rationale: During an active seizure, the nursing priorities are safety and observation: protect the head (soft padding), clear hazardous objects from the immediate environment, position on the side (lateral decubitus) to prevent aspiration when the seizure subsides, and time the duration. Nothing should be inserted into the mouth during an active seizure — this can cause injury to the patient and the nurse, and the jaw cannot be pried open safely. Physical restraint can cause musculoskeletal injury during tonic-clonic movements. Medication (benzodiazepine) is indicated for prolonged seizures (> 5 minutes, status epilepticus) — not every seizure automatically requires IV medication.

distractorRationales.a: "Insert an oral airway to prevent tongue biting and aspiration" misses the bedside risk. The cue "Active seizure: PROTECT (head, environment, airway position) → TIME → DO NOT insert objects in mouth, DO NOT" points to medication toxicity. Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.
distractorRationales.b: "Restrain the patient's limbs to prevent injury" misses the bedside risk. The cue "Active seizure: PROTECT (head, environment, airway position) → TIME → DO NOT insert objects in mouth, DO NOT" points to medication toxicity. Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.
distractorRationales.d: "Administer diazepam 10 mg IV immediately per standing orders" misses the bedside risk. The cue "Active seizure: PROTECT (head, environment, airway position) → TIME → DO NOT insert objects in mouth, DO NOT" points to medication toxicity. Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.

questions.takeaway: Active seizure: PROTECT (head, environment, airway position) → TIME → DO NOT insert objects in mouth, DO NOT restrain limbs. Post-seizure: lateral recovery position, assess airway, vitals, neuro. Administer benzodiazepines for status epilepticus (> 5 minutes).
